L147: For the first time, a reference map on board was used to compare with the descent images for lander localization during the terminal stage of EDL. It is critical that such a reference map have as little spatial and photometric error as possible. Photometrically, its representation should resemble as much as possible the descent images obtained by the spacecraft during EDL to allow easy and reliable terrain matching.
L148: Spatially, its local distortion (errors) relative to the true underlying terrain in both the horizontal and vertical directions should not introduce substantial error to the final localization solution. The Mars 2020 LVS team imposed the following requirements on this reference map (Table 【30†1】).
L149: Table 1. LVS Reference Map Requirements
L150: Requirements  | Description
L151: --- | ---
L152: Map generation  | The LVS map shall be a seamless and gap-free map composed of an LVS elevation map and co-registered LVS appearance map over at least the expected 99.7%tile landed ellipse determined by the time of the final site selection workshop with a buffer that extends 8 km radially beyond the boundary of the landed ellipse.
L153: Map projection  | The LVS map shall use an “orthographic projection” with square pixels of equal size to the local tangent plane of the Mars spheroid at the geometric center of the map.
L154: Map elevation definition  | The LVS elevation map shall define elevation as the perpendicular distance from Mars surface to the map local tangent plane.
L155: Map coregistration  | The LVS elevation and appearance maps shall be horizontally co-registered to within 6 m (99%) across the 30 × 30 km LVS map.
L156: Appearance map pixel size  | The LVS appearance map shall be 6 m/pixel and be derived from imagery with an optical resolution of no more than 6 m/pixel.
L157: Elevation map pixel size  | The LVS elevation map shall be 12 m/pixel and be derived from DEMs with a ground sample distance of no more than 20 m/pixel.
L158: Map absolute horizontal map tie error  | The LVS map shall have an absolute horizontal error in position in the map tangent plane that is less than 300 m with respect to the P inertial coordinate frame.
L159: Map absolute orientation error  | The LVS map shall have an angular error around the normal to the map tangent plane at the center of the map that is less than 1 mrad.
L160: Horizontal map distortion  | The LVS map shall have a horizontal distortion between any two pixels on the LVS map less than: 9 m (99%) for distances less than 120 m between pixels and18 m (99%) for all distances greater than or equal to 120 m between pixels, up to 12 km.
L161: Elevation map absolute elevation error  | The LVS elevation map shall have an absolute vertical elevation error less than 20 m (3 sigma) with respect to MOLA aeroid.
L162: Elevation map relative elevation error  | The LVS elevation map shall have an relative pixel to pixel elevation error less than 20 m (3 sigma).
L163: Appearance map signal to noise ratio  | The LVS appearance map shall preserve the SNR of the original radiometric corrected orbital images used to construct the appearance map
L164: Appearance map pre-processing  | The LVS appearance map shall be made from images that are radiometrically corrected but not enhanced, color balanced or smoothed to remove seams.
L165:   * Abbreviations: DEMs, Digital Elevation Models; LVS, Lander Vision System; MOLA, Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter.
L166: 
L167: These requirements would be trivial for Earth-based mapping. However, they present major challenges for Mars due to the following:
L168:   1. Lack of ground truth: For Earth based mapping, a high precision geodetic control network (GCN) for Earth covers most of the land surface. The precision of the GCN is on the order of millimeters (Bossler, 【31†1984】; Paar et al., 【32†2009】). However, the best Mars GCN is from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) and has a horizontal spatial scale of 128 pixel/degree (∼463 m/pixel) (Smith et al., 【33†2001】; Archinal et al., 【34†2004】).
L169: Although the MOLA data has sufficient vertical measurement accuracy (∼1 m; Smith et al., 【33†2001】), 463 m/pixel resolution cannot provide sufficient ground control for the 6 m/pixel LVS map. Furthermore, there is no direct ground truth measurements for Mars such as can be derived from GPS on Earth. Without these ground truth measurements, potential map errors such as map location error and local map distortion error are difficult to assess.

L167: These requirements would be trivial for Earth-based mapping. However, they present major challenges for Mars due to the following:
L168:   1. Lack of ground truth: For Earth based mapping, a high precision geodetic control network (GCN) for Earth covers most of the land surface. The precision of the GCN is on the order of millimeters (Bossler, 【31†1984】; Paar et al., 【32†2009】). However, the best Mars GCN is from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) and has a horizontal spatial scale of 128 pixel/degree (∼463 m/pixel) (Smith et al., 【33†2001】; Archinal et al., 【34†2004】).
L169: Although the MOLA data has sufficient vertical measurement accuracy (∼1 m; Smith et al., 【33†2001】), 463 m/pixel resolution cannot provide sufficient ground control for the 6 m/pixel LVS map. Furthermore, there is no direct ground truth measurements for Mars such as can be derived from GPS on Earth. Without these ground truth measurements, potential map errors such as map location error and local map distortion error are difficult to assess.
L170:   2. Noisy and error prone input imagery and ancillary data: Because of its compatible resolution (∼6 m/pixel) and coverage (∼30 km wide), the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) Context Imager (CTX; Malin et al., 【35†2007】) was chosen to make the LVS map. CTX was designed primarily to provide context for the high resolution (30 cm/pixel), but much smaller footprint High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE; McEwen et al., 【36†2007】).
L171: Because of this, some of the specifications for CTX fall short of the LVS map standard. For example, the existing CTX camera models contain significant, unaccounted radial distortion error. In addition, as with any pushbroom camera, knowledge error in spacecraft ephemeris and attitude are propagated to the two-dimensional map products derived from CTX images. As result, a ripple artifact (image jittering) can be present in CTX map products.
L172: Removal of this image jitter artifact is often very difficult and remains an open research problem (Mattson et al., 【37†2009】; Sutton et al., 【38†2017】; Che et al., 【39†2017】; Boyd et al., 【40†2009】).

L395: The atmospheric opacities are less than 1 except for one image (G13_023107). Overall, mosaic B is slightly better than mosaic A in term of τ values.
L396: We also investigated the consistency of the Orbit Determination (OD) solution. The SSD orbit determination is a batch process, in which a segment of time is processed at a time with small overlap between two adjacent segments. The orbit determination solution difference in overlap along range (R), in the tangent (T) direction, and in the normal (N) direction are used to assess reliability and accuracy of the OD solution.
L397: We found that all OD solution discrepancies for all CTX images are less than 10 m (Figure 【87†10】).

The R, T, and D discontinuity values at the time of CTX images were required to be less than 10 m. Data available through PDS.
L403: ### 2.6 CTX Image Time Tag Offset and Correction Procedure
L404: We observed that the RGs between any two stereo pairs of CTX images tend to be biased along the trajectory direction (left figure of Figure 【89†11】). This bias is generally under 20 m but in a few cases was observed to be more than 100 m. We also noticed that the bias is a function of the difference in acquisition time between the image pair. The longer the time between the two images, the more likely it is to have larger RGs in the uncorrected data.
L405: The reason for this apparent offset and its dependence on acquisition time is not fully understood. Two possible explanations could be temperature-induced flexure of the boresight alignment or CTX internal oscillator drift and potentially both. Testing of these hypotheses was outside the scope of this effort.

L582: ### 3.3 LVS Map Absolute Orientation Error
L583: 
L584: Requirements specify that the LVS Map shall have an angular error around the normal to the map tangent plane at the center of the map less than 1 mrad. We have conducted two tests.
L585: 
L586: First, we checked the map orientation difference among the LVS maps (both USGS and JPL maps) and HRSC map. We found that the angular difference between any LVS map is less than 0.2 mrad. The angular difference between USGS mosaic B and HRSC map is 0.8 mrad.
L587: Second, we tested the map orientation between the USGS mosaic B maps with an independent CTX image. In general, the MRO attitude error is much less than 1 mrad, therefore, we use the MRO attitude and individual CTX image row as a compass check on the local orientation. For each row of a CTX image, its projection onto the mosaic can be treated as the ground truth orientation, and its corresponding matched line in the map can be treated as the estimated orientation.

L199: ## 2 CTX Data Error Analysis and Removal
L200: ### 2.1 MRO/CTX Camera Model Validation and Refinement
L201: The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) Context Camera (CTX; Malin et al., 【35†2007】) is currently orbiting Mars and acquiring images at 6 m per pixel scale over a swath 30 km wide. Because its resolution and coverage are very similar to the LVS reference map and due to the relative abundance of available imagery, CTX was chosen to make the LVS reference map. First, we needed to evaluate the associated camera model. Prior to this work, two CTX camera models existed. The first is a model from Dr.
L202: James Bell (Bell 【49†2005】, 【50†2013】) on the MRO/CTX camera team and the second is a model from Dr. Randy Kirk at USGS (Semenov, 【51†2012】).
L203: The MRO/CTX camera team published the first CTX camera model (“Bell Model”) in (Bell, 【50†2013】). They used a collimated light source placed on top of a precision-controlled rotation stage to project a single vertical line onto the CTX focal plan. The autocollimator rotated in 1-degree steps through the CTX field of view and five measurement points were collected.
L204: Using the projected locations of the vertical light stripes on the CTX focal plan and the known angles from the precision rotation stage, a fifth order polynomial was fitted to the data to represent the mapping from angle space to pixels. This mapping is given by 2,502 + 872.37α + 0.877239α^{3} + 0.030α^{5}, where α is the angle (in degrees) from the optical axis.
L205: Observe that in this formulation, the model is symmetric about pixel 2502, which is the notional intersection of the optical axis with the focal plane in this model. Assuming 7 μm pixels, a simple linear fit yields a focal length of 351.14 mm. According to Bell (【50†2013】), the maximum amplitude of the distortion correction is 8–10 pixels at the edges of the CTX field of view.
L206: However, the formula above gives ∼15 pixels displacement at the edge of the image, which introduces up to an additional eight pixels of error (Figure 【52†1】).

L218: These two camera models not only differ in their representations but also in their distortion curves. The maximum difference between them is more than 40 pixels at pixel 5000, which equates to about 240 m on the ground. This was significant enough to warrant investigation.
L219: We took an approach suggested by USGS to refine the CTX camera model against other independent data. The MSL landing site, Gale crater, was chosen for this analysis. This was motivated by both existing repeat CTX image coverage and, more importantly, the descent image sequence from the MSL Mars Descent Imager (MARDI). Since MARDI is a frame camera and was carefully calibrated before launch, it provided a rare and valuable reference to study error in non-framing imagery such as from HRSC and CTX.
L537: The Jet Prolusion Laboratory (JPL) team made the first two independently constructed Lander Vision System (LVS) reference maps (A and B) for Jezero Crater site. These two maps are created from the top three pairs of Context Imager (CTX) images listed in Tables 【79†3】 and 【80†4】. The figure shows in order: the orthoimage mosaic for map A, the corresponding Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for map A, the orthoimage mosaic for map B, and the corresponding DEM for map B.
L538: The refined trajectory files, CTX camera pointing files and CTX camera model were converted into ISIS meta file format and were delivered to the USGS Astrogeology Science Center Team to make two LVS maps independently.
L539: ## 3 Final LVS Map Product Validation Procedure
L540: A great deal of effort was dedicated to developing procedures to validate the final LVS map. Because of the lack of ground truth, we rely heavily on consistency checks between independent data sources to identify potential errors. The JPL team used inhouse mapping software to make two LVS maps from two disjoint data sets.
L541: The USGS Astrogeology Science Center Team used traditional methods and the thoroughly validated SOCET SET software suite from BAE Systems to independently produce two maps using the same image data and JPL refined ancillary data and camera model (Fergason et al., 【126†2020】; USGS Astrogeology Science Center, 【127†2019】). The USGS team is the flagship institute for planetary mapping and has a long track record of success in making maps for planetary lander missions.
L542: The USGS map product was designated as the final LVS map product. In the meantime, we have additional data layers such as high-resolution HiRISE DEM/orthomap, HRSC DEM/orthomap, MOLA, and raw independent CTX images. Comparing the final LVS map against these different types of data products allows us to assess the final map quality from different aspects. The figure below shows the entire LVS map validation flow (Figure 【128†17】).

L548: ### 3.1 LVS Map Local Distortion
L549: 
L550: LVS requirements state that the LVS map shall have a horizontal distortion between any two pixels on the LVS map less than: 9 m (99%) for distances less than 120 m between pixels and 18 m (99%) for all distances greater than or equal to 120 m between pixels, up to 12 km.
L551: The local distortion is checked between two independent maps, namely, mosaics A and B. This process should reveal any errors intrinsic to the input images and their ancillary data as well as how effectively those errors were remove/reduced using the methods described above. Further, for the same input data, two maps each were made by the JPL and USGS teams using independent software chains. The comparison between these were expected to reveal any potential errors in procedure or methodology.
L552: Finally, a smaller, high resolution HiRISE map (ESP_048842_1985 &ESP_048908_1985) from USGS was expected to reveal any map distortion captured at higher fidelity than the CTX data. For any two maps, we used the following procedure to conduct the local distortion analysis
L553:   1. Construct delta feature flow map between the two studied maps. We used pseudo normalized correlation to find dense correspondences between orthorectified images. In addition, we added a small correction to compensate for the bias introduced by subpixel interpolation in the correlation process. We used a local homography outlier rejection scheme to remove any outliers. The pixel displacement maps are then converted into horizontal displacement fields in meters.
L554:   2. We then used the delta maps to compute the local distortion metrics. The local distance is defined as the delta distance between two points which are 120, 1,200, and 12,000 m apart in the first map and their corresponding locations in the second map. The local distortion histogram and mean standard deviation are computed in this way (Figure 【130†18】).

L579: ### 3.2 LVS MAP Absolute Horizontal Map Error
L580: The USGS team also estimated a final horizontal transform to move the LVS appearance map into better alignment with the HRSC DT5 orthoimages. The CTX LVS map products in the orthographic projection (both DEM and orthoimages) were shifted 17.9614 m west and 20.2454 m north in order to bring them into better alignment with the HRSC ND5 reference orthoimage. After the shift, the mean delta x and delta y maps between the LVS and HRSC map are close to zero.
L581: This shift also improved the agreement between the LVS DEM and the HRSC DEM vertically.
L582: ### 3.3 LVS Map Absolute Orientation Error
L583: 
L584: Requirements specify that the LVS Map shall have an angular error around the normal to the map tangent plane at the center of the map less than 1 mrad. We have conducted two tests.
L585: 
L586: First, we checked the map orientation difference among the LVS maps (both USGS and JPL maps) and HRSC map. We found that the angular difference between any LVS map is less than 0.2 mrad. The angular difference between USGS mosaic B and HRSC map is 0.8 mrad.
L587: Second, we tested the map orientation between the USGS mosaic B maps with an independent CTX image. In general, the MRO attitude error is much less than 1 mrad, therefore, we use the MRO attitude and individual CTX image row as a compass check on the local orientation. For each row of a CTX image, its projection onto the mosaic can be treated as the ground truth orientation, and its corresponding matched line in the map can be treated as the estimated orientation.
L588: The angle between the two fitted lines is a good indicator of the orientation error. We used an independent CTX image (F04_037398_1985_NX_18N282N), which is not part of the map process, to test USGS mosaic B, the delta angle values are shown in the right image of Figure 【138†22】. All angle errors are significantly smaller than 1 mrad.

L594: ### 3.4 LVS Elevation Map Absolute and Relative Elevation Error
L595: The LVS map elevation was also shifted vertically to the HRSC map. A systematic vertical offset (∼190 m) has been found in multiple Mars 2020 candidate landing sites during the LVS map construction using the same procedure proposed here. The exact reason of this offset is still unknown.
L596: After adjusting the mosaic by 183.3 m vertically to align with HRSC, the LVS elevation map has a median vertical displacement relative to the HRSC DT5 reference of 1.88 m which is well below the 20 m absolute vertical error requirement.
L597: We have also studied the relative vertical error. The dz map between the JPL mosaics A and B is shown in Figure 【128†17】. The one sigma of dz is 4.35 m and the 99th percentile of relative elevation error between these two maps is 13.05 m, which is better than the 20 m mission requirement. The difference between USGS mosaic B and JPL mosaic B is also well within the mission requirement.
L598: The MOLA tracks over Jezero crater were also used to test the relative and absolute elevation error. For each MOLA point, we calculate the delta elevation between the MOLA point and the computed DEM. The mean delta z is 0.215 m with standard deviation of 9.67 m. The large standard deviation is mainly due to the large footprint of MOLA (200 m) versus the 20 m CTX DEM resolution over high terrain relief areas. The lower picture in Figure 【140†23】 shows the discrepancy between MOLA points and LVS elevation.
L599: The size of dots in the right image are proportional to the delta z. We can observe that large delta z happens at areas of high terrain relief as expected. If those areas are excluded from calculation, the standard deviation is reduced to 7 m, which is very close to the 20 m (3 sigma) requirement.

L167: These requirements would be trivial for Earth-based mapping. However, they present major challenges for Mars due to the following:
L168:   1. Lack of ground truth: For Earth based mapping, a high precision geodetic control network (GCN) for Earth covers most of the land surface. The precision of the GCN is on the order of millimeters (Bossler, 【31†1984】; Paar et al., 【32†2009】). However, the best Mars GCN is from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) and has a horizontal spatial scale of 128 pixel/degree (∼463 m/pixel) (Smith et al., 【33†2001】; Archinal et al., 【34†2004】).
L169: Although the MOLA data has sufficient vertical measurement accuracy (∼1 m; Smith et al., 【33†2001】), 463 m/pixel resolution cannot provide sufficient ground control for the 6 m/pixel LVS map. Furthermore, there is no direct ground truth measurements for Mars such as can be derived from GPS on Earth. Without these ground truth measurements, potential map errors such as map location error and local map distortion error are difficult to assess.
L185:   5. Compare the final map product with other maps: By comparing the LVS map with other maps from different platforms such as the High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) (Neukum et al., 【44†2004】) aboard the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, MOLA or from the HiRISE instrument aboard MRO, we expected to add evidence of validity to the LVS map. None of the maps or data is perfect and all of have strengths and weaknesses.
L186: For example, the MOLA data has the most accurate vertical range measurements, but its spatial resolution of ∼400 m/pxl is low. HiRISE has the best spatial resolution (∼1 m), but its spatial coverage is small. HRSC has larger spatial coverage, but its resolution (12.5 m/pixel) and map quality are not as high as needed. However, in combination, these disparate data sources serve to validate various aspects of our process.
L187: Specifically, we use MOLA to evaluate absolute elevation error, HRSC to test the absolute map position, and HiRISE to assess local distortion and relative elevation error.

L605: ## 4 Conclusions
L606: 
L607: In this paper, we presented a series of improvements and advancements for making a reference map from CTX imagery for the Mars 2020 LVS. The final LVS reference map quality meets or exceeds the mission requirement due to four major improvements and breakthroughs.
L608: 
L609:   1. We have recalibrated the CTX camera model. The new camera model significantly reduces the camera model error from 100s meters to less than 6 m and map orientation error from 1.5 to 0.3 mRad.
L610:   2. By analyzing the RGs errors from CTX stereo image pairs, relative time offsets between them were found and corrected. A time correction is added to each CTX image, resulting in RG error reduction to less than 5 m, down from an uncorrected 10–100 m.
L611: 
L612:   3. We have developed a new pushbroom bundle adjustment method to correct spacecraft (s/c) pointing errors. This new algorithm effectively reduces the RG error induced by s/c jitter from ∼5 m to less than 2 m, 1-sigma.
L613:   4. We took into account multiple criteria including image coverage, viewing angle, atmospheric opacity, image quality, orbit determination solution accuracy, and mars orientation model in selecting the most suitable image sets and ancillary data.
L614: Two independent Jezero maps have been produced. We have conducted a map distortion comparison between the two maps with and without these four improvements and found that the map error has been reduced about seven-fold after applying them. Without these improvements, the map error would have been significantly greater than the mission requirement. We have conducted multiple validations including a cross check between the two maps as well as between CTX and HRSC, HiRISE, and MOLA.
L615: All these validation results indicate that we have successfully made the first ever LVS reference map for the Mars 2020 mission.
